Title: 'Football will never be the same without my brother,' says teen after fatal lorry accident
Article:
KUALA TERENGGANU: A 14-year-old boy was left traumatised after witnessing his 8-year-old brother being struck and killed by a lorry while retrieving a football in Kampung Surau Haji Daud yesterday.
Muhammad Idham Najmi Mohd Asizol said he could only cry when he saw his younger brother, Muhammad Atihff Zriqqiz, lying on the road.
"I was shocked and cried when I saw my brother lying on the road. I can still vividly recall the incident," he said when met at the forensic department of Sultanah Nur Zahirah Hospital last night.
The Form Two student of Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan Tengku Ismail said he had been playing football with Atihff and their 12-year-old brother, Muhammad Ammar Najwan, inside their fenced compound at about 3pm.
However, tragedy struck when the ball bounced over the fence and across the road.
"My brother ran out to fetch the ball before he was hit by a lorry passing along the village road," he said.
"It will no longer be fun playing football because my brother is gone."
Atihff, a Year Two pupil at Sekolah Kebangsaan Kubang Ikan, died at the scene in the 3.40pm accident along Jalan Surau Cik Man.
https://www.nst.com.my/news/regional/2026/10/1557647/boy-8-dies-after-being-hit-lorry-while-retrieving-ball
Meanwhile, their father, Mohd Asizol Wahab, said the accident happened about 15 minutes after he left home for work as a courier delivery driver.
He said he had eaten with Atihff before leaving at 3pm to deliver parcels around the village.
"Fifteen minutes later, my wife called to tell me that our son had been hit by a lorry in front of our house. I rushed home and found him lying motionless on the road," he said.
Atihff was buried at the Haji Idris Family Cemetery in Kampung Tok Adis, Kuala Ibai, at 1.30am today.

Title: #NSTviral: Boy wins hearts for guiding blind elderly man at LRT station
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A young boy has won hearts online after he was seen guiding a blind elderly man at Maluri LRT station, helping him navigate the station safely.
Threads user @syifanadine92 shared the moment, praising the boy's kindness.
"May all the goodness you give find its way back to you, kind soul," the user wrote.
The post drew warm responses from other users, many of whom shared similar experiences of helping visually impaired people in public.
One user, @careyryan_, recounted helping a blind man exit an MRT station despite being late for a train.
"Although I was late for my train, I helped the man exit the station.
"As I went down the escalator, another man, whom I believe was a doctor, chased after me, tapped me on the shoulder and thanked me for helping before running back upstairs.
"It really made my day," the user wrote.
Another user, @ieya.az, praised the gesture, writing: "Such a beautiful soul. May he always be blessed!"
View on Threads
Meanwhile, @hi_mayahhhhh said they had witnessed a similar scene at Pasar Seni LRT station, where a young man helped a blind elderly man by asking him to place his hand on his shoulder as they chatted.
"May the goodness in your heart lead you to beautiful things," the user wrote.
Another user, @panadol_cat_, said people in their neighbourhood often helped blind residents cross roads, including those who walked about 20 minutes to reach the MRT station.

Title: Pasir Gudang records country's highest API reading at 190, 25 areas unhealthy
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Pasir Gudang in Johor recorded the highest Air Pollutant Index (API) reading in the country at 190, as 25 areas nationwide registered unhealthy air quality as of 8am today.
Johor was the worst-hit state, with eight of its monitoring stations in the unhealthy category.
According to the Department of Environment's Air Pollutant Index Management System portal, the other affected areas in Johor were Larkin (181), Kota Tinggi (181), Pengerang (178), Batu Pahat (169), Kluang (163), Tangkak (160), and Segamat (157).
In the Klang Valley, Johan Setia recorded 163, followed by Shah Alam (161), Klang (159), Petaling Jaya (157), and Banting (156). In Kuala Lumpur, Cheras recorded 156, and Batu Muda registered 155, while Putrajaya logged 159.
The readings came despite heavy rain in the Klang Valley over the past few days.
In Negri Sembilan, Nilai recorded 172, followed by Seremban (169) and Port Dickson (152). Melaka's Bukit Rambai, Alor Gajah, and Bandaraya Melaka recorded 164, 161, and 155, respectively.
In East Malaysia, Sandakan and Serian each recorded 153, while Tawau registered 103.
Only Limbang in Sarawak (45) and Balik Pulau in Penang (42) recorded good air quality.
Yesterday, Pasir Gudang recorded a very unhealthy reading of 203, with Johor remaining the state hardest hit by the haze.
Readings between 0 and 50 are categorised as good, 51 to 100 as moderate, 101 to 200 as unhealthy, 201 to 300 as very unhealthy, and 300 and above as hazardous.

Title: 'My sister's face looked peaceful,' says brother of murdered Customs officer
Article:
TUMPAT: "Although there were slight wounds on the side of her face, she looked peaceful," said the brother of Norhazwani Ibrahim, who was believed to have been killed by her husband in Nilai, Negri Sembilan, last Thursday.
Mohd Hazwan Ibrahim, 38, said he was overcome with emotion when he saw his sister's face for the final time after her shroud was opened.
"Her face looked calm. I am relieved that everything has been settled," he said when met after the burial at the Tanjung Muslim Cemetery here at 1.50am today.
"After two days, Wani's remains have finally been safely laid to rest."
Norhazwani, a Customs officer who had transferred to the Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) scheme, was stationed at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA).
It was previously reported that she was allegedly stabbed by her husband at their home in the KLIA quarters in Nilai on Thursday.
She suffered two stab wounds to the left abdomen and one to the right cheek.
The
suspect surrendered
to police shortly after the incident and was remanded for seven days from yesterday to assist investigations under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder.
A post-mortem found that Norhazwani died from pressure applied to her neck.
Negri Sembilan police chief Datuk Alzafny Ahmad said the cause of death was determined following a five-hour post-mortem at the Forensic Medicine Department of Hospital Tuanku Ja'afar yesterday.
He said physical examinations also found
three stab wounds
caused by a sharp weapon — two to the abdomen and one to the right cheek.
About 200 people, comprising family members, MCBA personnel, Customs Department personnel, police officers and local villagers, attended the funeral.
Also present were MCBA deputy director-general (Operations) Datuk Mohd Nasaruddin M. Nasir and Tumpat police chief Assistant Commissioner Mohd Khairi Shafie.
Hazwan said he and his family were focusing on settling the remaining matters, including the tahlil prayers, for now.
He said they had yet to decide on long-term plans for Norhazwani's two daughters, aged five and six.
"They were already under the care of my elder sister here previously. So, we intend to keep them with us," he said.

Title: Trump paused Russia sanctions to 'analyse' impact on global economy: Rubio
Article:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump's waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to "analyse" their impact on the global economy.
"The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.
He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they're having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices" but on economies as well, he said.
US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticised Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia – measures adopted by Congress last month.
The law passed in September, and signed by Trump, included sanctions targeting Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and provided Trump with the authority to impose sanctions on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
The idea was to cut off sources of funding to supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as his war on Ukraine.
But late Friday, two days before the law was due to take effect, Trump exempted Russia from those economic restrictions.
"Beyond irresponsible," Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent Trump critic who will leave office in January, said in a post on X.
"If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."
Ted Cruz, a senior Republican senator from Texas, called the move "a mistake" in comments aired on Fox News.
Trump's executive order came after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions.
The impact of steep diesel price hikes due to the Iran war are beginning to filter into the US economy, and cost of living worries are top of mind for voters ahead of key midterm elections next month.
Polls show Trump's Republicans are likely to receive a drubbing at the polls.
"The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were (going to) make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," Rubio said, underscoring the importance of the vital fuel powering US road hauling, agriculture and construction.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that Trump's action "rewards" Putin.--AFP

Title: Zelenskyy says Trump could lift more Russia sanctions
Article:
KYIV: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that President Donald Trump's action only "rewards" Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Trump heightened a battle with Zelenskyy on Friday when he signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions targeting Russia's energy revenues.
The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine in the fifth year of its war, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Trump had already announced that he has agreed a deal with Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions, and Zelenskyy said he feared more concessions.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters.
He said he still "personally" hoped that Trump will do "everything in his power" to make Putin end the war but added: "You cannot achieve this by limiting Ukraine's responses to Russia for killing our people. And certainly not by lifting sanctions."
Ukraine said at least two people were killed in Russian air strikes on Saturday.
- 'Pressure' needed -
Zelenskyy said the US decision on Friday came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in "one of the largest" attacks on Ukraine's energy grid.
Officials said one person was killed in the southern city of Kherson in an attack that also wounded 22 people, including two children, and that another was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
Zelenskyy said the US decision on Friday came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in "one of the largest" attacks on Ukraine's energy grid.
The Lindsey Graham Act – named after the late US senator who sponsored the bill – targeted Russia's energy and defence sectors, as well as Putin and the so-called "shadow fleet" of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent Western sanctions.
"It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening," Zelenskyy said on social media.
The Lindsey Graham Act, he said, was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end" adding that the act "could have helped enormously – and still can!".
"A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," he warned.
The Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to cause a "blackout" in Ukraine ahead of winter: "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating." He called on allies to pressure Moscow to "stop this."
Last winter saw hundreds of thousands in Ukraine consistently without heat and electricity in freezing temperatures.
- RUSSIA HAILS TRUMP MOVE AS 'HISTORIC' -
The Kremlin and Putin have not yet reacted to Trump, but several Russian officials celebrated the move as a win.
"The Trump administration's suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump announced the sanctions waiver in an executive order Friday, shortly after Putin appeared in military uniform and said Moscow aims to capture the rest of east Ukraine.
US-led talks to end the war have failed to bring a breakthrough.  Putin and Zelenskyy have frustrated Trump in the past.
Zelenskyy rallied his allies Friday on a visit to Brussels for a European Union summit, urging them to keep financing Ukraine's fight and insisting he was standing up for his country amid the row with Trump.
- PUTIN VOWS MORE -
Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defences ahead of winter.
Russia controls large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine by force.
"On the whole I see a positive trend in the operations of the troop groupings," Putin told army leaders Friday, dressed in military attire.
"Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People's Republic," he added, using the Kremlin's name for the eastern Donetsk region. --AFP

Title: 19 killed, 25 injured in stampede at India's Durga Puja festival
Article:
KOLKATA: At least 19 people were killed and two dozen more injured Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that occurred during sudden rainfall at a Hindu religious gathering, officials and Indian media said.
West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl, adding that 25 other people were injured outside a pavilion "in a stampede" at the Hindu festival of Durga Puja in the city of Kolkata.
"Six bodies have so far been identified," Adhikari said.
A senior police official at the scene told AFP an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining at night and the "crowd waiting outside the pandal (pavilion) was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede."
Afterwards medics were seen moving injured people on stretchers, including a police officer, into a local hospital. Several relatives of victims cried and held one another as they mourned the loss of loved ones.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the tragedy in a short statement on Facebook.
"The stampede in Kolkata is saddening. Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery," he wrote.
"The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families."
Adhikari originally announced 17 fatalities. The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported the death toll rose by two to 19, quoting Adhikari in a later statement.
Nine dead bodies have been released to their families, the PTI reported.
It also said police have taken the closed circuit footage of the festival and authorities would initiate action against those seen on CCTV who appeared to fail in their responsibility for crowd control.
Videos shot before the stampede appeared to show large crowds of people waiting to enter the pavilion, in an area with narrow lanes that allow only a few people to walk in at a time, according to Indian Express.
Deadly crowd incidents are a frequent occurrence at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, due to poor management and safety lapses.
Last year, a stampede at India's Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others, and 11 fans were crushed to death in Bengaluru during celebrations for the local cricket team's first Indian Premier League title.
The same year, 36 people were killed after a stampede broke out at a campaign rally of a popular actor-turned-politician in southern Tamil Nadu state.
In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering.--AFP

Title: Protecting kids from AI menace
Article:
CYBERJAYA: The misuse of artificial intelligence (AI) to create sexually explicit images, particularly of children, is on the rise, prompting calls for stronger safeguards and closer parental supervision.
Multimedia Content Forum of Malaysia (CMCF) chief executive officer Mediha Mahmood said AI tools could be used to turn images of people into sexually explicit materials or deepfake videos in inappropriate situations.
"It is not an authentic image. It is a manipulated image or deepfake video altered by AI to depict the victim in a sexual or inappropriate manner," she said recently.
Mediha said the growing use of AI tools by children is another concern, as unrestricted applications and websites may make it easier to create illicit content.
"The most glaring issue is the proliferation of unrestricted apps, websites and open-source tools that can be repurposed for these malicious purposes.
"There are so many of them," she said.
She said easy accessibility of these applications has made it difficult to monitor or control the use of AI platforms.
"These AI-generation platforms cannot always be fully monitored or controlled. Most concerningly, they are accessible to anyone with a connected device, without verifying whether the user is an adult or a child.
"Access remains largely unrestricted for minors and other vulnerable groups," she said.
Mediha said distributing sexually explicit material involving children is an offence under the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017, even if the person circulating it is a minor.
[[nid:1557873]]
"This is a critical point that must be impressed upon parents, guardians, teachers and anyone who interacts regularly with children."
She said Malaysians have embraced AI for creativity and efficiency, but malicious users have taken advantage of the technology.
"Like any other service or application, bad actors will exploit and manipulate it.
"We see amazing uses of AI for creativity and efficiency. But because it is available to everyone, we also see bad actors using it for nefarious purposes," she said.
Mediha said existing laws, including the Penal Code, the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 and the Online Safety Act 2026, may be used to address AI misuse.
However, gathering digital evidence is a challenge for enforcement agencies.
She called on those who have fallen victim to AI manipulation or those aware of such incidents to lodge reports with the police and relevant agencies.
She said even after the online content has been taken down or deleted, this does not mean that the evidence can no longer be recovered.
"People often assume that once a link is deleted, nothing more can be done.
"But in discussions with enforcement agencies, such as the police and the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC), there are technical avenues to recover links and trace digital forensic evidence.
"People should not assume an incident cannot be reported. Reports can and should be filed, and action will be taken," she said.
Mediha said digital platforms should adopt the "Safety by Design" and "Safety by Default" principles.
They include restricting certain image-manipulation features for minors and requiring verifiable consent before images can be altered.
While social media platforms have been working with MCMC to comply with regulatory frameworks and licensing requirements, she said collaboration with generative AI providers remains limited.
"From CMCF's perspective, there has not yet been meaningful collaboration, largely because engaging these independent AI developers and providers is quite difficult."
Mediha said the problem is not a lack of legislation.
"Rather, it is a lack of awareness among parents who do not fully grasp the potential harm their children face.
"It is fundamentally an advocacy and digital literacy issue," she said.
She cited MCMC's Internet Selamat (Safe Internet) campaign as an initiative to educate parents about online risks, platform safety features and how to configure them.
"Parents need to understand the threats, learn about the safety features offered by platforms and know how to configure them," she said.
Mediha wants parents to supervise their children's use of AI applications, particularly when providing them with Internet-connected devices or devices with recording capabilities.
"Whether they like it or not, if parents provide Internet-connected devices or devices with recording capabilities to their children, they must ensure the usage is supervised," she said.
She added that the government's stand of not allowing children under 16 to open social media accounts should serve as a benchmark for other online services.
Mediha said preventing AI misuse requires shared responsibility among regulators, enforcement agencies, digital platforms, parents and the wider community.
"We also need everyone to help these children understand the grave dangers of using AI to generate inappropriate imagery of themselves or their peers and sharing it."

Title: Underwater mountains, canyons hold secrets of Malaysia's seas
Article:
PORT KLANG: Beneath Malaysia's vast maritime waters lies a dramatic landscape of underwater mountains, ridges, valleys and canyons, much of which remains unmapped to modern hydrographic standards.
National Hydrographic Centre (NHC) director-general Rear Admiral Dr Najhan Md Said said understanding this hidden terrain was vital to safe navigation, maritime security and sovereignty.
"If you drain the water from the South China Sea, you will see a terrain just as breathtaking as anything on land.
"There are underwater mountains, massive ridges, steep trenches and ancient riverbeds that once ran above water thousands of years ago," he told the New Sunday Times.
Najhan also serves as the vice-chair of the International Hydrographic Organisation — Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans Sub-Committee on Undersea Feature Names, comprising 12 international experts.
The sub-committee is responsible for establishing internationally consistent nomenclature and naming guidelines for undersea features, ensuring uniformity across nautical charts, bathymetric maps and scientific publications worldwide.
He said high-resolution bathymetric surveys had mapped extreme depths across Malaysia's maritime domain.
[[nid:1557944]]
Seabed mapping, he added, shared some principles with astronomy, but also carried a strong connection to national identity and heritage.
"When astronomers discover a new star, individual scientists are often allowed to put their names on it. But under international maritime rules, individuals cannot name undersea features. That privilege belongs strictly to sovereign nations.
"To date, Malaysia has secured official recognition for 17 undersea feature names, most of them in the bathymetrically rich waters off Sabah and Sarawak," he said.
The New Sunday Times was provided with advanced 3D acoustic renderings from the NHC, showing the varied topography of some seabeds in Sabah and Sarawak.
Among them are the Santubong Seamount, a jagged, volcanic-like spire; Kenyalang Hill, with its sharp, conical summit; and the Rafflesia Hill, a massive dome-shaped mound.
Measured against the Kuala Lumpur skyline, the seabed's peaks hold their own.
Santubong Seamount rises about 1,400m from the ocean floor, roughly twice the height of Merdeka 118, the country's tallest building. Yet its summit lies about 500m below the surface.
Rafflesia Hill, at about 450m, matches the Petronas Twin Towers, while Kenyalang Hill, at about 320m, is 100m shorter than KL Tower (421m).
Rungus, Kadazandusun and Bidayuh Hills each rise about 900m, a third taller than Merdeka 118.
Submerged mountain chains include Iban Ridge, Bajau Ridge and Kimaragang Ridge, which stretch across the ocean floor.
The seabed also features deep chasms and valleys, including the steep-walled Meranti, Chengal and Anggerik canyons, and the broad, flat-bottomed Mawar Valley.
Najhan said naming undersea features has helped preserve Malaysia's cultural identity, with internationally recognised names documenting the country's heritage on global maps and in scientific records.
"Through ongoing high-resolution bathymetric surveys, the NHC has identified and prepared another 45 undersea features for formal registration and submission to the sub-committee on undersea feature names.
"Imagine looking at an international ocean gazetteer or a global map and seeing an underwater mountain in your home waters named in a foreign tongue.
"It feels like a personal sting to national pride," said Najhan.
He added that hydrographers had a duty to not only map the seabed, but also ensure its features bore the names reflecting Malaysia's history, culture and identity.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: National Hydrographic Centre seeks legal status to safeguard Malaysia's maritime interests
Article:
PORT KLANG: Malaysia needs a dedicated national hydrography act to give its hydrographic authority statutory backing and replace a 54-year-old administrative memorandum that can be amended or rescinded by the cabinet.
National Hydrographic Centre (NHC) director-general Rear Admiral Dr Najhan Md Said said despite operating for more than half a century and representing Malaysia in the International Hydrographic Organisation (IHO) since 1975, the centre is still relying on a cabinet memorandum produced in 1972.
He said an act of Parliament was needed to establish the NHC as the sole national authority responsible for official nautical charting, bathymetric data governance and maritime safety declarations.
"Without a statutory foundation, the NHC faces administrative hurdles that hamper its agility, as even routine operational and inter-agency approvals require lengthy administrative processes.
"Enacting the National Hydrography Act will give the NHC institutional permanence, streamline decision making and provide long-term funding stability," he told the New Sunday Times.
[[nid:1557791]]
Najhan said the proposed law would give the national hydrographic authority formal legal recognition and strengthen its ability to maintain continuous maritime domain awareness, safeguard navigation and protect Malaysia's maritime interests.
"For more than 50 years, the NHC has operated under a 1972 cabinet memorandum rather than a formal Act of Parliament. Administrative memorandums remain legally fragile because any sitting cabinet can amend or rescind them."
He said national reviews, including the Royal Commission of Inquiry  into Batu Puteh, had recommended a national hydrography act to replace the existing administrative framework and give the NHC explicit statutory authority to fulfil its national responsibilities.
"Under the proposed legislation  which has received support from the Defence Ministry and its policy division, the NHC is envisioned as a standalone department directly under the ministry, similar to the Veterans Affairs Department and the Science and Technology Research Institute for Defence.
"It would report directly to the defence minister, while operational personnel would continue to be drawn from the Royal Malaysian Navy."

Title: Smoke trail, flames offer clues to Long Lellang helicopter crash
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Examination of the Flying Doctor Service's Bo-105 helicopter engines, and a video of flames and smoke near the rear of its main gearbox captured during the helicopter's final moments near Long Lellang, Sarawak, could help investigators establish what happened, an aviation expert said.
This follows the release of the Air Accidents Investigation Bureau's (AAIB) preliminary report yesterday, which found no fault with the crashed helicopter's airframe, maintenance or pilot.
Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School Associate Professor Major Dr Mohd Harridon Mohamed Suffian said a thorough examination of the engines was standard procedure to help investigators determine the likely cause of the incident.
"Dissection of aircraft components is needed to acquire the flight's wear-and-tear history, where it would tremendously aid investigators in their logical structuring of the incident.
"Stripping down the engine would allow each component to be scrutinised for patterns of malfunction and show whether its function was impeded during flight.
"The extent of damage could also be measured in detail, allowing investigators to pinpoint the nature of the incident," he added  when asked on the preliminary report.
The AAIB report also stated that the engines had been sent to the manufacturer's facility for further examination, adding that any airworthiness implications for other engines of the same type had yet to be established.
The helicopter was fitted with two Rolls-Royce 250-C20B engines manufactured in 1989 and 1976.
On the AAIB's findings of a visible smoke trail and apparent flames near the rear of the main gearbox, as well as substantial fire and impact damage, Harridon said investigators would examine burn patterns and damaged components to determine where the fire started and how it spread.
"The rear section of the Bo-105 houses several critical components, including the exhaust system, fuel and hydraulic lines, tail rotor drive shaft and transmission system.
"Investigators will  examine burn patterns to determine where the fire started and how it spread.
"Scorch marks and chemical traces on damaged components could also help establish the sequence of events. If the fire is intense, heat can spread quickly in different directions."
He added that the fire could affect the helicopter's flight controls, transmission and structural integrity, making it important to establish how it spread and whether it contributed to the crash.
"During an emergency, a rapid succession of problems may leave pilots with little time to react. Even if the initial signs appear minor, pilots must assess the situation carefully, as it could escalate into a more serious emergency."
In George Town, Transport Minister Anthony Loke said the final report on the helicopter crash was expected to be published within a year.
On Sept 8, a Flying Doctor Service Bo-105 helicopter carrying five people crashed near Long Lellang STOLport in Sarawak, killing all on board.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: One survey ship falls short of mapping Malaysia's vast maritime domain [WATCH]
Article:
PORT KLANG: Only 63 per cent of Malaysia's vast maritime domain has been surveyed to modern high-density hydrographic standards, leaving 37 per cent yet to meet the benchmark.
Modern high-density hydrographic surveying refers to mapping the seabed in a comprehensive, accurate and high-resolution detail to produce nautical charts.
National Hydrographic Centre (NHC) director-general Rear Admiral Dr Najhan Md Said said surveying Malaysia's maritime domain was a major undertaking requiring extensive work to build a comprehensive picture of the seabed.
"Many people do not realise the true extent of Malaysia's maritime territory.
"In reality, our maritime domain is almost twice the size of the land mass we typically draw on maps, spanning 569,845 sq km," he told the New Sunday Times in an exclusive interview.
He said Malaysia's breakthrough came in 1998, when KD Perantau, a hydrographic survey vessel, began its service.
Switching from a single-beam to multi-beam echo sounder, the technology transition had enabled a comprehensive, accurate and higher-resolution seabed mapping process.
[[nid:1557808]]
In 2018, the decommissioning of naval survey vessel KD Mutiara then left KD Perantau as the NHC's sole hydrographic survey ship.
Now, the ageing vessel faces limitations in covering Malaysia's vast maritime domain alone.
FLEET CONSTRAINTS
Najhan said surveying the remaining 37 per cent of the country's waters to modern high-density standards with a single ship is challenging.
"Relying on a single naval survey ship to complete high-density mapping across our entire maritime domain would take an estimated 55 years.
"Expecting one vessel to cover the waters off Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak is impossible," he said.
[[nid:1557807]]
To ease the shortfall, Najhan said the National Security Council (NSC) had introduced a three-year strategic outsourcing programme, allocating RM30 million annually to lease commercial hydrographic survey ships.
"Before this NSC-funded contract took effect, modern survey coverage had not even reached 50 per cent.
"Through outsourcing, we doubled our surveying pace and raised modern coverage to 63 per cent.
"However, national security imperatives require a dedicated fleet of naval survey vessels."
TRADE AND SOVEREIGNTY
Najhan said hydrographic surveying was critical not only to navigation, but also trade, economic security and maritime sovereignty.
The stakes are high for Malaysia, whose economy depends heavily on maritime trade.
"Data from the Academy of Sciences Malaysia indicates that the nation's ocean-based 'Blue Economy' contributes 21.3 per cent to the national gross domestic product, or roughly RM300 billion in 2020.
"Yet, the public frequently overlooks the ocean's immense economic and strategic importance," he said.
Najhan added that hydrographic surveys could help authorities maintain accurate nautical charts by detecting changes in seabed depth and identifying underwater hazards.
"The absence of sufficiently detailed or updated data does not necessarily make an area unsafe to navigate, but it can limit the accuracy of information available to mariners and authorities responsible for navigational safety."
He cited the Strait of Malacca, where the NHC determines and verifies depth parameters for the global shipping standard known as Malacca Max.
"Commercial mega-vessels traversing the Strait of Malacca operate under strict draft limits of 22 to 23.
"However, heavy maritime traffic may continually shift the seabed sand dunes, making shallow areas even shallower over time.
"Global shipping lines rely on the NHC to ensure that declared draft limits on nautical charts are accurate.
"If a mega-vessel ran aground because of inaccurate depth charts, the economic fallout would extend beyond Malaysia and could bring global trade to a standstill," he said.
Malaysia's maritime depths vary widely — from 110m northwest of Pulau Perak in the northern Strait of Malacca, to 2,932m east of Permatang Ubi, Sabah, in the South China Sea.
[[nid:1557806]]
Beyond navigation, seabed surveys provide scientific evidence of underwater features within Malaysia's maritime domain.
These support their identification and naming through international scientific processes.
However, where maritime sovereignty or jurisdiction is contested, hydrographic data must be considered alongside the relevant legal framework and other supporting evidence.
However, seabed mapping alone does not establish ownership of maritime territory.
Najhan said bathymetric data on submerged mountains, ridges and valleys was crucial when responding to foreign submissions to name undersea features through international bodies, such as the Sub-committee on Undersea Feature Names.
"Under international protocols, if a foreign entity attempts to register undersea features outside of our territorial waters but within Malaysia's Maritime Zones, we cannot simply object verbally. We must present our own verified bathymetric survey data.
"Accurate, updated hydrographic data provides Malaysia with the technical evidence needed to register native feature names and assert its maritime sovereignty."
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Israeli settlers beat French mayor with iron bars, attack European diplomats in West Bank
Article:
JERUSALEM: Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked a convoy of European diplomats in the West Bank and beat up a visiting French mayor, witnesses said, a day after an American photographer was similarly set upon as violence escalates ahead of bitterly fought elections.
The 78-year-old mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.
"I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, told AFP after he was attacked.
"The whole world needs to know what's happening," he said. "For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here."
Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack but he did not need hospital care.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a statement that Israel must "urgently halt criminal violence" and arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux, with his Belgian counterpart issuing a similar call.
- ELECTION SEASON -
The attack came just one day after settlers beat an American photographer for The Washington Post, who was in moderate condition on Saturday after suffering broken vertebrae.
Israel's foreign ministry condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to shore up support from the fiercely pro-settlement far-right in the Oct 27 election, instead alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.
Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause.
"We urge caution before drawing conclusions" about the attacks, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
His main rival in the elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was "burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses."
The attacks are "Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government", Eisenkot said.
- ATTACKS ON CULTURAL SYMBOL -
Baudoux, the mayor, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement.
He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol.
Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians' annual harvest after months of escalating attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property. There has also been violence against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting a settler dead last month.
Bashar Fawadleh, a priest in Taybeh, said settlers had already attacked the harvest and snatched olives before beating the mayor.
"One person was hit in the head and needed stitches. They also beat up an older lady in her 70s after insulting her with very bad words," the pastor told AFP.
The West Bank violence has shocked much of the world, with Britain spearheading economic sanctions that in turn led Israel to close the British consulate in Jerusalem.
Netanyahu had also sought to throw doubt on the circumstances behind the beating Friday of the photographer, Heidi Levine, suggesting that Palestinians and "far-left" activists caused trouble.
But President Isaac Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, took the initiative Saturday to call Levine in the hospital, saying the attack was "outrageous and shocking" and weighed on his conscience.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee said the beating was "a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards", and demanded Israel prosecute and jail the assailants.
Israel Gantz, head of an umbrella settler group, blamed recent incidents on "groups of provocateurs and terrorists" but implicitly acknowledged some Israelis' responsibility, saying that they harmed the settlers' cause.
Settlers earlier this month also beat up AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he covered the olive harvest tensions, fracturing several of his ribs and stealing his camera.
Netanyahu's government has ramped up approval of West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
Some 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel seized in 1967, alongside three million Palestinians.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: US demands jail for attackers of American journalist in West Bank
Article:
JERUSALEM: US Ambassador Mike Huckabee on Saturday demanded that Israel prosecute and jail the assailants in a West Bank settler attack against a Washington Post journalist.
"Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards," Huckabee wrote on X, taking a far stronger tone than an earlier statement from Washington.
Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has nonetheless sharply criticised settler attacks against Americans, did not identify the culprits as settlers, after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu tried to sow doubt as to their identity.
"Details of who under investigation, but those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend (years) in prison," Huckabee said.
"We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this."
Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer, was taken to hospital with broken vertebrae. She was listed on Saturday as being in moderate condition.
She had been covering Palestinians' annual harvest of olives, which has been repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers.
Settlers beat her and stole her passport, telephone, wallet and equipment, according to witnesses.
Netanyahu, who wants to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base ahead of close-fought Oct 27 elections, on Friday insisted that Palestinians or "far-left" activists may have been responsible.
The US State Department on Friday took a cautious tone on Levine's beating, saying It condemns "criminal violence by any party."--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: France protests erupt into looting and fires as 1,200 arrested, 150 police hurt
Article:
PARIS: Clashes between police and protesters, massive looting and multiple blazes gripped France on Saturday, as nationwide marches against soaring inflation degenerated into street violence of "extreme intensity."
The widespread unrest follows weeks of student protests and deepens political uncertainty as the country readies for elections in six months' time to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Whole streets in Paris "have been devastated", the city's mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said as groups of masked young men torched parked cars and ransacked many shops.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who earlier slammed the "violence of extreme intensity", said late Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt.
The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities over the cost of living that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people participated.
Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne.
- LOOTING IN MANY CITIES -
During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.
Scores of shops – supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetic vendors and consumer electronics stores – were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.
AFP reporters in Paris saw groups of half a dozen young men often attacking the shops in an organised way: wearing masks and gloves, they first disconnected security cameras before smashing windows to get in.
The looting added to a day of destruction and vandalism, with town halls in several cities targeted.
The one in the city of Limoges – more than 140 years old – was largely destroyed by a blaze set by masked protesters who broke in, according to the region's top official. Two others were broken into and vandalised in Marseille and Lille.
A police compound in Bordeaux was also vandalised, while in Lyon protesters set ablaze a tourist office.
Macron vowed on X that "those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting – even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."
Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in presidential elections in April and May seized on the chaos.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned "the rioters" and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, had "legitimised the violence."
She said on X that, if she came to power, she would protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left."
Melenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests preceding them, urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods."
- A 'REVOLUTION' -
France's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
But there were other issues too.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign."
High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons – the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years."
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
"It's the Revolution – we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry of the mayor's offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death."
And in the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" was unfurled above a central square.
"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Saudi Arabia intercepts four drones as Egypt weighs defensive support
Article:
RIYADH: Saudi Arabia said on Saturday that it had intercepted a fresh wave of incoming drones, as its ally Egypt weighed sending the kingdom help in defending against repeated attacks from Yemen's Houthis.
Riyadh leads a military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government in its war with the Houthis, and a military spokesman for the Iran-backed group said Saturday that dozens of Saudi strikes over the past day had killed and wounded "numerous" people.
Since Yemen's conflict flared back to life in July after a years-long hiatus, Saudi Arabia has faced sustained Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its oil installations, tankers and transit hubs, including one on Riyadh's airport last week that killed 13 people.
A spokesman for the Saudi coalition said on Saturday that it had "intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in the regions of Riyadh, the Eastern Province, and the South."
The interceptions came as the president of Egypt, which is also a member of the coalition, said he was willing to "carry out any measure to protect" Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt was not looking to intervene in regional wars, but added that it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while the kingdom was "harmed or its security and stability threatened."
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," he said. "We are speaking only about defence."
Though Egypt is a member of the anti-Houthi coalition, its role has mostly concerned Red Sea maritime security rather than the fighting in Yemen.
It and Saudi Arabia are historically close and have strategic economic ties.
Egypt's parliament will hold an emergency session on Sunday at Sisi's request.
The repeated Houthi strikes have prompted foreign embassies to warn their citizens not to use Saudi airports, or not to visit the country altogether.
The Saudi education ministry on Saturday announced the extension of remote learning measures for students in Riyadh and nearby Diriyah.
Residents of the Saudi capital received a mobile phone alert early on Sunday warning of a "hostile aerial threat" and to stay away from windows and doors. It was lifted after a few minutes.
- 'POLITICAL PROCESS' -
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis' recent escalation, a charge Tehran denies.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran supported a "comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve" the conflict on the Arabian Peninsula.
He also repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides.
Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture.
But Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba rejected Iran's offer in a statement on X Saturday, saying "the Teheran regime is a party to the war against Yemenis, not a mediator."
The Houthis are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, but both they and Teheran insist the group acts independently.
Saudi Arabia has carried out daily airstrikes on the Houthis in Yemen, where government forces are seeking to roll back gains the group made in a lightning offensive in September.
On Saturday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Riyadh had conducted 53 strikes in the capital Sanaa and six other provinces over the past 24 hours, causing "numerous dead and wounded."
A Houthi-affiliated news agency had earlier accused Saudi warplanes of targeting "civilian residences" in Dhamar and Taiz provinces, killing 12 people and wounding more than 30.
It alleged that the strikes were carried out "using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally."--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Indonesian fisherman found off Tioman repatriated
Article:
JOHOR BARU: An Indonesian fisherman who went missing after becoming separated from the boat carrying his two children has been repatriated after being found adrift in waters off Pulau Tioman, Pahang.
The Indonesian Consulate General in Johor Bahru worked with the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) in Pahang on the search and rescue operation following a missing-person report received by Indonesian authorities.
Consular Officer Dhania Afini Lestari said Bachtiar, from the Anambas Islands regency in the Riau Islands, underwent a medical examination after being rescued and received temporary accommodation and supplies.
He was escorted by MMEA Pahang personnel and handed over to Indonesian border authorities at the maritime boundary between the two countries at 5pm today, she said in a statement.
Bachtiar was reported missing on Oct 10 after becoming separated from the boat carrying his two children while they were fishing. His boat had run out of fuel, and food supplies were depleted before he was found safe in waters off Pulau Tioman on Thursday.
The consulate urged fishermen to ensure their boats were seaworthy, carry sufficient fuel and food, and have navigation and communication equipment before going out to sea.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: No explosives found at Klang supermarket after bomb threat
Article:
KLANG: Police found no explosives or suspicious devices at a supermarket along Jalan Kapar here following an email claiming that such materials had been planted on the premises.
North Klang police chief Assistant Commissioner Ramsay Embol said police received a report at 4.04pm today from a male store manager who had received the email.
He said police inspected the premises with assistance from the K9 sniffer dog unit, the Selangor police contingent headquarters' bomb disposal unit, the fire and rescue department and the Klang civil defence department.
"After an inspection lasting nearly three hours, police and the assisting teams found no explosives or suspicious devices as claimed in the email," he said in a statement today.
Ramsay said the case was being investigated under Section 507 of the Penal Code, which concerns criminal intimidation by anonymous communication and carries a penalty of up to two years' imprisonment upon conviction.
He advised the public against using email or other forms of communication to spread information that could threaten public order and cause fear in the community.
Anyone with information on the case can contact the North Klang district police headquarters at 03-32919614 or the investigating officer, Inspector Mohd Fazlan Rezza Mazlan, at 011-10561017.
Earlier, several social media posts went viral claiming that a supermarket in Klang had been closed following the discovery of a bomb on the premises.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: 24 evacuated after floods hit eight Penang houses
Article:
BUKIT MERTAJAM: Twenty-four residents were evacuated to a temporary relief centre after heavy rain flooded eight houses in Kubang Semang.
Penang Fire and Rescue Department assistant operations director John Sagun Francis said firefighters assessed the situation near Masjid Kubang Semang after receiving a call at 9pm.
Firefighters arrived at 9.10pm and found floodwater had entered the houses, reaching an estimated knee-high level.
The residents were evacuated by police to the temporary relief centre at Sekolah Kebangsaan Seri Penanti, which opened at 8.30pm.
Water levels were receding.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Clashes erupt in France as protesters vow to make government 'tremble'
Article:
PARIS: Police and protesters clashed in Paris and other French cities on Saturday, with smoke from fires and tear gas billowing over demonstrations nationwide against high prices ahead of elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Masked youths set a tourism office in Lyon ablaze, as riot squads resorted to tear gas and water cannon to disperse hundreds of people confronting them.
In Marseille, France's second-largest city, protesters broke into the town hall, overturning a bust and smashing furniture before being forced out by police, AFP journalists saw. The mayor called for police reinforcements.
In the northern city of Lille, protesters smashed their way into the mayor's office and vandalised the premises before leaving.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign".
"For years we've had climate, economy and equality problems but the government is not doing anything about it," said Agnes, a 50-year-old actor who did not give her second name, as she marched.
High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons – the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years".
Yellow Vest movement
The windows of the offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in western Paris were broken by protesters, and AFP journalists saw several parked cars torched.
Police in the capital fired water cannon and tear gas when hundreds of protesters wearing face masks, some setting off fireworks, confronted them at several locations, AFP reporters saw. More than 130 people were arrested in the capital, police said.
The country's Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests against Macron's government eight years ago over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for the "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website set up by organisers.
In Paris, authorities banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations.
Many demonstrators complained about inflation, which had soared above three per cent amid the war in the Middle East.
Others criticised perceived police brutality during student protests that have gripped France over the past four weeks.
The combined unrest from both protest movements has created a febrile climate as the country heads towards presidential elections in six months' time.
Le Pen blames 'rioters'
Opposition politicians vying to succeed Macron have seized on the protests.
Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who has sided with the police, said on X: "Looting, pillaging, attacking police – rioters have once again sullied the October 17 demonstrations over the cost of living."
She claimed that the protesters' demands had been "hijacked by the far left".
[[nid:1557702]]
Her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon, for his part, insisted that "everything is passing off peacefully" in most of the nationwide demonstrations, while accusing television news of "flooding us with images of violence in dozens of cities".
Macron on Friday urged "respect for people and property".
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
"It's the Revolution – we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry into the mayor's offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death."
In the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" was unfurled above a central square.
"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.
'Suffocating' from inflation
The soaring cost of living has become a major concern for the French, worrying around 45 per cent of them, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.
"At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren't," said Franck, a civil servant in his forties who would not give his surname, as he demonstrated in the central town of Gueret with around 300 people, a quarter of them high school students.
"We can't take it anymore, we're suffocating," he added.
Purchasing power in France has dwindled since 2024, while fuel prices have soared since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year.
The eurozone's second-largest economy is struggling to rein in its public debt, which is projected to exceed 120 per cent of GDP next year — double the European Union limit of 60 per cent.

Title: Man found dead in drain in Penang
Article:
BUKIT MERTAJAM: Police recovered the body of a 52-year-old man from a drain near Taman Ciku here.
Authorities received a call about the discovery at 4.30pm, and firefighters were deployed to retrieve the body.
Initial investigations found that the man had died less than 24 hours earlier.
The body was sent to Bukit Mertajam Hospital for a post-mortem.
Police investigations are ongoing.

Title: Hanoi's famous flowers are driving residents mad with their smell
Article:
THE star-shaped white blossoms of Hanoi's milkwood trees have inspired songwriters and lovers, but city authorities began cutting them back on Friday after an outcry from residents over their "overpowering" fragrance.
The Vietnamese capital boasts more than 14,400 Alstonia scholaris, tall evergreens that shade the streets in summer and in autumn, produce flowers that fill the air with a heady scent.
For many residents, it is too much.
"The smell is so overpowering that it becomes unpleasant, especially when the weather is hot," resident Tran Trung Phong said.
The 56-year-old said he keeps his doors and windows shut and suffers from headaches and breathing difficulties as his four-storey home comes "under direct attack" from dozens of trees nearby.
"If it were up to me, I would replace them all," he said.
His complaint is similar to those made across social networks and reported in state-run media in recent days, prompting Hanoi authorities to take action.
On Friday, they began a drive to prune up to 1,000 trees along 13 streets to reduce their intense fragrance.
The trees are common across much of Asia.
In Vietnam, where they are known as hoa sua, they are evoked in nostalgic or romantic songs and poems about Hanoi.
But a poll conducted by state-controlled online newspaper VnExpress found 80 per cent of respondents supported removing or relocating the trees.
"Only those who don't live near these trees find them romantic with a pleasant fragrance. Try it for just one day. You will hate it forever," wrote Thanh Luong on Facebook.
She said her bedroom is located about 100m away from two trees, adding: "It's torture."
The evergreens, which reach more than 10m tall, are synonymous with Hanoi - so much so that they have been planted in areas of central and southern Vietnam as a way to import some of the capital's charm.
For resident Lan Huong, they are key to the city's identity, and also provide a welcome flash of nature in polluted streets.
"Hoa sua is the signature for Hanoi. Everyone knows and accepts that as a fact," she said.
"Isn't breathing in the scent of flowers far more pleasant than inhaling smokes from bikes and cars?"
City authorities on Thursday said the trees were a "signature feature of autumn in Hanoi, contributing to the city's distinct urban identity".
But they acknowledged the smell "negatively impacts the health and lives of residents, as well as the quality of the living environment".
They said they will consider whether they can "relocate some of these trees to more suitable locations and replace them with other types of greenery".
In 2019, around 100 hoa sua trees were relocated to the city's outskirts.
But a similar plan in 2023 to shift away 80 from a main street failed due to objections from locals, state media reported.
"I feel sorry... for hoa sua being denounced at this autumn trial," wrote Loi Phan Mai in a Facebook post that drew thousands of positive reactions.
"It is easy to cut down a tree, but how does one go about cutting down a memory? How could a hoa sua tree possibly be guilty?"
The writer is from AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Six women honoured at YTF Women in Technology Awards 2026
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Raja of Perlis, Tuanku Syed Sirajuddin Jamalullail, and the Raja Perempuan of Perlis, Tuanku Tengku Fauziah Tengku Abdul Rashid, graced the Yayasan Tuanku Fauziah (YTF) Women in Technology Awards 2026 here today.
The awards presentation and gala dinner were held in conjunction with Tuanku Tengku Fauziah's 80th birthday celebration.
Also present were the Raja Muda of Perlis, Tuanku Syed Faizuddin Putra Tuanku Syed Sirajuddin Jamalullail, and the Raja Puan Muda of Perlis, Tuanku Dr Lailatul Shahreen Akashah Khalil, who is also YTF Royal Patron.
Academician Emeritus Professor Datuk Dr Aini Ideris led the six women recognised for their contributions to technology, research, innovation and leadership.
Aini, a former Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) vice-chancellor, won the grand prize in the Senior Women in Technology category, receiving RM30,000.
Universiti Teknologi Petronas (UTP) associate professor Dr Serene Lock Sow Mun won the grand prize in the Junior Women in Technology category, receiving RM15,000.
In the senior category, UPM senior lecturer professor Dr Suraya Abdul Rashid received the Special Award – Rising Star, while Global Psytech founder Dr Haniza Yon was named Industry Changemaker. Both received RM10,000 each.
In the junior category, Universiti Malaya senior lecturer Dr Marlinda Ab Rahman received the Special Award – Rising Star, while Universiti Malaysia Sarawak associate professor Dr Afzan Ahmad Zaini was named Industry Changemaker. Each received RM5,000.
The awards recognise women's contributions to technology, raise their visibility and inspire the next generation to pursue excellence in science, technology and innovation.
Members of the YTF Board of Trustees, distinguished guests, and representatives from industry, academia and the technology sector were also present.

Title: Road to an all-electric car fleet will be bumpier than it looks
Article:
The global shift to electric vehicles (EVs) might appear unstoppable, but the path there is far from straightforward.
Battery EVs will eventually dominate passenger car fleets across every region, according to global risk management firm DNV, and will capture more than 90 per cent share by 2050 in markets ranging from China and Europe to Southeast Asia.
That might appear to signal a rapid decline in oil demand for road transport, and merit steep downward revisions in gasoline consumption forecasts across major regions.
However, a closer look at the inventory data for the underlying car fleets suggests the journey away from internal combustion engines (ICE) likely has plenty of twists and turns ahead.
The fuel outlook is clouded by the fact that some countries are moving faster than others to replace ICE cars with EVs, while others are expanding EV fleets alongside sales of conventional cars.
China is the undisputed heavyweight of global electrification, and the country's electric car fleet is already greater than that of the rest of the world combined, with around 37.5 million passenger EVs in use, DNV data shows.
By 2035, DNV projects that over 165 million EVs will be on China's roads, before the total tops 360 million by 2050.
China's vast EV manufacturing base, integrated battery supply chain and extensive charging network continue to drive down ownership costs and accelerate adoption.
Beijing has also rolled out subsidies for EV purchases and mandates for automakers to accelerate the shift away from fuel-burning vehicles.
The region with the largest projected decline in ICE cars by 2050 is Europe, where conventional car numbers are seen contracting from around 284 million currently to about 77 million, DNV's projections show.
Policies designed to cut transport emissions alongside a constantly expanding fleet of charging stations are making EVs a more attractive choice among car buyers.
And even though conventional cars still outsell EVs made by European carmakers, sales numbers of EVs and hybrids suggest that customers are keen to switch to EVs as they become increasingly affordable and convenient.
Reversals in policies around EVs and federally-funded charging systems have dented the sales growth of EVs in North America in recent years, and look set to result in a slower fleet transition away from ICE cars compared to other major car markets.
North America's fleet of ICE cars is around 290 million, and conventional engines account for around 86 per cent of the total car fleet.
By 2040, however, ICE cars are expected to number around 215 million and account for only 30 per cent of the total fleet thanks to a projected boom in EV uptake from around eight million cars currently to nearly 86 million.
Steadily declining costs of EV ownership alongside improved access to charging stations are expected to drive EV uptake in North America, even though access to relatively cheap petrol looks set to keep ICE cars on the road for longer.
The Indian subcontinent is still expanding its fleet of ICE passenger cars, estimated at around 73 million and will top out at around 165 million in the late 2040s.
Limited charging infrastructure and consumer concerns about costs are expected to delay the region's upswell in EV uptake into the 2050s.
That said, electric scooters and motorcycles are seeing rapid growth in the region, and should promote continued expansion of charging infrastructure and greater electric grid stability that will underpin the eventual EV-heavy swing in car trends.
Car buyers in Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America and the Middle East are expected to follow similar paths, with sales of ICE cars seen expanding into the 2040s before EVs emerge as the dominant choice.
China and Europe appear set to remove well over 300 million ICE passenger cars from their roads between now and 2050, leading to a major long-term decline in petrol demand in those regions.
However, declines in ICE car numbers are likely to be partly offset by continued growth in conventional vehicle ownership in India and other emerging markets over the coming decades.
The destination is clearly a more electrified global vehicle fleet, but the speed of the journey remains far less certain.
The writer is from Reuters
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Kelantan policeman injured in parang attack during anti-drug raid
Article:
TANAH MERAH: A police corporal was seriously injured after being slashed with a parang by a suspected drug pusher during an anti-drug operation in Kampung Lalang Pepuyu.
Kelantan police chief Datuk Mohd Yusoff Mamat said the 37-year-old officer suffered a fractured left hand in the 1.35pm incident and was admitted to Hospital Tanah Merah.
He said a team from the Kelantan police contingent headquarters' Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID), assisted by personnel from Bukit Bunga and Lalang Pepuyu police stations, raided a house in the village.
The suspect, a local man in his 30s, tried to flee after seeing the officers but swung the parang at them during a chase, injuring one officer before being arrested.
Police seized the 35cm parang, 0.1g of suspected yaba pills and a bottle of liquid believed to be ketum juice.
Mohd Yusoff said the suspect had six previous drug-related offences.
The case is being investigated under Sections 307 and 324 of the Penal Code, Section 12(2) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 and Section 30(3) of the Poisons Act 1952.
The arrest was part of Ops Tapis Bersepadu Sempadan, an integrated operation aimed at curbing drug smuggling and distribution along the Malaysia-Thailand border.
